summary:
Mozambique's legal position on consensual same-sex conduct is among the more permissive in sub-Saharan Africa. The 2015 Penal Code erased the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision, and same-sex conduct has been legal since. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on the basis of identity or consensual conduct.

No procedure for legal gender recognition exists in Mozambican law. A visitor whose passport or other documents carry markers inconsistent with their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at checkpoints and in any interaction requiring identification. The sources describe no formal screening process, and they offer no assurance against one.

The Penal Code (Law 24/2019, in force from 2020) contains hate-crime and hate-speech provisions with direct bearing on trans visitors. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on grounds of gender identity, and also covers defamation, insults and threats directed at transgender people. Article 160 treats a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating factor in homicide. Enforcement of these provisions is not documented in the sources.

Protection machinery exists in limited form. Applications by Lambda Mozambique, the country's only LGBT organisation, were blocked from 2008 onward, prompting a UN appeal in 2010. In October 2017 the Constitutional Council struck down the 'moral order' clause of Article 1 of Law No. 8/91 that had been used to refuse registration, and on 28 November 2017 it ruled that the organisation's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment. Employment protections that had been in place since 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024. The Advertising Code of 2016 separately bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships; same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. Reports from Lambda describe a community that is not subjected to the levels of targeted violence seen in some other African states but does face routine discrimination, family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education.
tangentialFactors:
Afrobarometer data reported in 2016 placed Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant societies: 56% of respondents said they would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, against 5% in Uganda, Burkina Faso and Niger.

Public opinion on relationship recognition is more divided than the legal position suggests. A 2017 survey found support for same-sex marriage at 47% in Maputo, 38% in Beira and 42% in Nampula, and a 2017 ILGA poll found 61% of Mozambicans agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as heterosexual people. The same 2017 ILGA poll found 55% of respondents believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

The same surveys record hostility beneath those figures. Most respondents in the 2017 survey said they would not accept a child who came out, and 28% of Beira respondents said they would assault their child if he or she was gay. Offsetting that, 85% opposed violence against LGBTQ people and said they would intervene if such a person were being physically assaulted, and about one-third of respondents personally knew an openly LGBTQ person. A 2013 survey found moderate support for LGBTQ parenting rights.

Political turbulence affects expectations. The 2024 election-cycle pledge by the opposition party PODEMOS raised expectations within the LGBT community and then disappointed them. Protests demanding same-sex marriage and common-law union recognition have run since 2006.

Early organising took place under the colonial-era statute; a rights argument first appeared in the press in 2006 and the LGBT group remained unregistered as of 2011, with the decade-long registration battle ending only in 2017.
localsOnly:
Residents face discrimination rather than prosecution. Lambda Mozambique's own assessment is that the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination; the sources record hate crimes and violence against LGBTQ people as rare while discrimination is common.

Workplace protection that existed from 2007 was removed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024, leaving residents without a non-discrimination claim in employment, and none in education, health or housing either.

Family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education are the everyday form of disadvantage reported for LGBTIQ residents. Society is broadly neutral in attitude, according to Outright International's March 2026 assessment.

Same-sex couples have no route to marriage or adoption, and no partner or spousal recognition of any kind exists in Mozambican law.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the instrument that removed employment non-discrimination protection: Outright International attributes the removal to a 2024 penal code, while other material attributes it to Labor Law No. 13/2023. Which instrument governs is unresolved here.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 chapter on Mozambique, published 11 January 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests but contains no transgender-specific content and no information on where trans prisoners are housed. Prison placement for trans detainees is not sourced.

No source in this inventory addresses border or immigration screening of gender markers, entry refusal on those grounds, access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors, or facilities and restroom access. Whether enforcement bodies apply Articles 160 and 190 in practice, and how police handle an identity-document mismatch, are likewise not documented.
